tier_reason: lzbench 2.4 README table (public benchmark code github.com/inikep/lzbench, bench/lzbench.h codec table) lists bzip2 1.0.8 -1/-5/-9 next to ppmd8 26.03 -1/-4/-9 and lzma 26.03, run with the gcc 15.2.0 release binary on a single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P; the public Makefile builds bzip2, ppmd and lzma objects with -O3 -DNDEBUG (mk/bzip2.mk and mk/ppmd.mk set no -O2 override). Same A treatment as the other lzbench 2.4 entries (wave 9 retier-02).

corrections.license: bzip2-1.0.6 (the 'bzip2 and libbzip2 License v1.0.6', a permissive BSD-style licence, as shown on the GitLab page and API); the SPDX licence list (3.29) marks bzip2-1.0.6 as not OSI-approved; no patent grant
corrections.stars_or_usage: GitLab project bzip2/bzip2 (now titled 'bzip2-archived', archived): 93 stars, 27 forks; GitHub mirror libarchive/bzip2 (a clone of an earlier GitLab repo) has 64 stars and 34 forks; bzip2 1.0.8 tag dated 2019-07-13; the system bzip2 library of essentially every Linux distribution
corrections.caveats: The speed claim against PPM is not in the code repository: the manual in this repo (docs/manual.xml) only says compression 'approaches the performance of the PPM family of statistical compressors' and itself recommends zlib or LZO for anyone wanting something faster. The figures 'within 10% to 15% of the best available techniques (the PPM family), whilst being around twice as fast at compression and six times faster at decompression' come from the bzip.org project description, seen only as a WebSearch snippet repeated on HPC documentation sites (bzip.org and sourceware.org are blocked here). lzbench reproduces the decompression half (2.5x to 14x faster than ppmd8 depending on level) but not the compression half (level with ppmd8 -4, 1.2x slower than ppmd8 -1 at similar size). The comparison is against one PPMd implementation (7-Zip PPMd var.I), and ppmd8 -4 gives a 6% smaller output. bzip2 is slower or larger than modern codecs in the same table (lbzip2 2.6.5 -9 compresses 22.4 MB/s and decompresses 47.0 MB/s at the same size; lzma 26.03 -4 and zstd 1.5.7 -18 reach similar or smaller outputs at 26.39% and 25.14% while decompressing 73.7 and 1175 MB/s, though zstd -18 compresses at only 4.13 MB/s). The GitLab repository is the archived 1.1+ development fork ('archived due to lack of interest, and because there are better options available through the Rust ecosystem'); its last commit is 2023-05-31 and it carries the bzip2-1.0.8 tag (2019-07-13), so the benchmarked 1.0.8 sources are in this repo as well as at sourceware.org. Licence is a permissive BSD-style text that SPDX does not list as OSI-approved, so usability follows the non-OSI rule (reference); no patent grant. The record fills the project's slot; its value is as the reference implementation, not as a fast codec.

notes: Numbers match the lzbench 2.4 README rows exactly and the derived ratios check out (35.5/11.5 = 3.1x, 35.5/14.0 = 2.5x, 35.5/2.55 = 13.9x decode; 12.7 vs 12.8 MB/s compress). Fixed last_commit (2023-05-31 from the GitLab API; the repo also holds the 1.0.8 tag) and set usability to reference because SPDX marks bzip2-1.0.6 not OSI-approved (precedent: BSD-3-Clause-Clear set to reference); the orchestrator may override that since the licence is BSD-style permissive. Shortcomings: archived repo, compression not faster than PPMd, slower or larger than lbzip2, lzma and zstd in the same table, 2x/6x project claim seen as snippet only.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 729 stars, 87 forks; shipped as a 7-Zip codec plugin per the README; built into lzbench
corrections.caveats: The lzbench 2.4 README run (-eALL preset) includes only LZHAM levels -0 and -1, although lzbench registers levels 0-4 (bench/lzbench.h); the default uber level and the extreme parser were not run, so the README's 'ratio similar to LZMA with 1.5x-8x faster decompression' is only partly reproduced: LZHAM -1 beats lzma -4 and -2 on size and decode speed, but lzma -6 and -9 outputs are 9.5% and 11.1% smaller than LZHAM -1 (LZHAM -1 is 10.5% and 12.4% larger; derived from page data), and LZHAM -1 compresses 4.3x slower than lzma -4. The README's own 10GB-benchmark figures (7zip-LZHAM 9.38 32-bit, 64 MB dictionary: LZHAM -mx=9 3,573,782,721 bytes with archive test time 71.292 s vs LZMA -mx=9 3,560,052,414 bytes at 223.050 s, about 3.1x) carry no hardware or compiler and mattmahoney.net is blocked here. The README also says the decoder is slower than zlib's and only overtakes LZMA's above roughly 1,000-13,000 compressed bytes, so it is a poor fit for small blocks. The improved branch richgel999/lzham_codec_devel is already in the catalogue at tier C on that README evidence; this record is the stable v1.x repository, the one lzbench links and builds. The most recent commits (2022-01-03) only edit README.md; code last changed around the 2020-09-15 public-domain relicensing. Public-domain dedication (LICENSE, 2020-09-15): no patent grant. The listed code.google.com/p/lzham URL is the old alpha and was not opened.

notes: lzbench rows match exactly (lzham -1: 3.16 / 273 MB/s, 54,740,589 bytes; lzma -4: 13.6 / 73.7 MB/s, 55,936,064 bytes; 273/73.7 = 3.7x). Corrected two caveat details: lzbench supports LZHAM levels 0-4 (only the -eALL README run is limited to -0/-1), and the lzma -6/-9 size gap is 9.5-11.1% smaller rather than '10-12% smaller'. Same project as already-verified richgel999/lzham_codec_devel (tier C, README evidence only); the orchestrator may fold the devel id into this one (or record duplicate on one of them), since this id carries the stronger lzbench evidence.

tier_reason: First-party run printed in the python-blosc README from its public script bench/compress_ptr.py, with CPU (Xeon E5-2695 v3) and thread count stated but no compiler flags for the C library (only the Python interpreter's GCC 4.4.7 banner); partial methodology, so C, not A or B.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; official Python wrapper (python-blosc, 362 stars) and HDF5 filter (hdf5-blosc); the README says c-blosc is in pure maintenance mode and recommends C-Blosc2 for new work
corrections.caveats: The numbers are the project's own, printed in the README of the Python wrapper (python-blosc 1.5.1.dev0 driving Blosc 1.11.2, a 2017 run) from bench/compress_ptr.py, with partial methodology: CPU and thread count are stated, the compiler flags of the C library are not (the header only shows Python 3.5.2 built with GCC 4.4.7). Each figure is a single time.time() measurement with no repetitions, and the 'GB/s' figures are GiB/s (N*8/t/2**30); decompressed output is checked with an assert. The memcpy baseline is one single-threaded ctypes.memmove call on the arange array while Blosc ran 24 threads, so the ratio mixes parallelism with compression. All three inputs are highly compressible: arange and linspace are synthetic linear sequences (ratio up to 260x with bitshuffle), and the 'random' distribution is np.random.randint(0, 1001) stored as int64 (about 10 significant bits per 8-byte element), not incompressible data. Without shuffle blosclz is slower than memcpy. The c-blosc2 repo's own bench/results-corex/blosclz-suite-corex.out (Blosc 2.0.0.beta.6.dev, 2020, no CPU named, 4 MB synthetic data with 19 significant bits, blosclz+shuffle) shows the same shape: at 1 thread and clevel 1, decompress 10667.6 MB/s vs memcpy(read) 8289.1 MB/s and compress 4714.6 vs memcpy(write) 4628.8 MB/s. The blosc.org benchmark pages and the 2010 CISE paper are EGRESS_BLOCKED here, so they were not read. c-blosc is in pure maintenance mode (README); the Blosc2 successor (github.com/Blosc/c-blosc2) is already in the catalogue at tier C.

notes: Numbers match the python-blosc README exactly (memmove 0.276 s, 2.70 GB/s; blosclz+shuffle arange 17.77 / 27.18 GB/s; random lz4+shuffle 11.02 / 26.03 GB/s; 6.6x and 10x derived ratios correct). Added harness facts from bench/compress_ptr.py: single-shot timings, GiB units, and the 'random' input is randint(0, 1001) int64, so every dataset is very compressible. Shortcomings: single-threaded memcpy vs 24-thread Blosc, synthetic data, no compiler flags, maintenance mode; not a duplicate of c-blosc2 (separate 1.x library and format), but related.
